class="hover:text-blue-400 text-xs md:text-sm whitespace-nowrap author-name" href="/security-labs/author/jia-yu-chan">Jia Yu Chan</a><span class="mx-2">•</span><a class="hover:text-blue-400 text-xs href="/security-labs/author/terrance-dejesus">Terrance DeJesus</a></div><h1 class="font-bold leading-tighter text-3xl md:text-5xl"><span>TCLBANKER: Brazilian Banking Trojan Spreading via WhatsApp and&nbsp;Outlook</span></h1><p class="text-zinc-200 text-base md:text-xl">REF3076 uses a trojanized Logitech installer to deploy TCLBANKER, a Brazilian banking trojan with environment-gated payloads, WPF fraud overlays, and self-propagating WhatsApp and Outlook worm modules.</p><div class="flex items-center mt-4 text-zinc-200 text-sm space-x-4 border-t border-white/25 pt-4"><span class="flex items-center space-x-1"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" stroke-width="1.5" stroke="currentColor" aria-hidden="true" class="h-4 w-4 text-zinc-400"><path stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" d="M12 6v6h4.5m4.5 0a9 9 0 11-18 0 9 9 0 0118 0z"></path></svg><span>18 min read</span></span><span class="flex items-center space-x-1"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" stroke-width="1.5" stroke="currentColor" aria-hidden="true" class="h-4 w-4 text-zinc-400"><path stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" d="M9.568 3H5.25A2.25 2.25 0 003 5.25v4.318c0 .597.237 1.17.659 1.591l9.581 9.581c.699.699 1.78.872 2.607.33a18.095 18.095 0 005.223-5.223c.542-.827.369-1.908-.33-2.607L11.16 3.66A2.25 2.25 0 009.568 3z"></path><path stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" d="M6 6h.008v.008H6V6z"></path></svg><span><a class="hover:text-blue-400 whitespace-nowrap" href="/security-labs/category/malware-analysis">Malware Analysis</a>, </span><span><a class="hover:text-blue-400 whitespace-nowrap" href="/security-labs/category/threat-intelligence">Threat Intelligence</a></span></span></div></div><div class="lg:max-w-7xl mx-auto relative mt-12 lg:grid lg:grid-cols-4 lg:gap-8 items-start"><div class="flex lg:col-span-3"><div class="prose lg:prose-lg prose-invert w-full article-content"><div><p>Elastic Security Labs identified a new Brazilian banking trojan that we are tracking as TCLBANKER, a malware family we assess is a major update of the <a href="https://securelist.com/maverick-banker-distributing-via-whatsapp/117715/">MAVERICK</a>/<a href="https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/j/self-propagating-malware-spreads-via-whatsapp.html">SORVEPOTEL</a> family. The campaign, tracked as REF3076, features a loader with robust anti-analysis capabilities that deploys two embedded .NET Reactor-protected modules: a full-featured banking trojan and a worm module for self-propagation.</p>
<p>The banking trojan monitors the victim&#x27;s browser address bar via UI Automation, targeting 59 Brazilian banking, fintech, and cryptocurrency domains. Beyond the usual remote access commands, its most notable capability is a WPF-based full-screen overlay framework designed for operator-driven social engineering.</p>
<p>A second module handles distribution through spam agents, of which we recovered two variants: a WhatsApp worm that hijacks authenticated browser sessions to message the victim&#x27;s contacts, and an Outlook email bot that sends phishing emails through the victim&#x27;s own accounts via COM automation.</p>
<p>Through this report, we provide a detailed technical breakdown of each stage.</p>
<h2 class="font-bold text-2xl md:text-4xl relative"><span id="key-takeaways" class="absolute -top-32"></span>Key takeaways</h2>
<ul>
<li>TCLBANKER uses environment-gated payload decryption; incorrect environments, such as sandboxes, silently fail to decrypt the payload</li>
<li>A comprehensive watchdog subsystem continuously monitors for analysis tools, debuggers, instrumentation frameworks, and integrity violations throughout execution</li>
<li>The banking trojan targets 59 Brazilian banking, fintech, and cryptocurrency domains, activating a WebSocket C2 session when a victim navigates to a monitored site</li>
<li>A WPF-based full-screen overlay framework enables operator-driven social engineering, including credential harvesting, vishing wait screens, and fake Windows Update stalls, while hiding overlays from screen capture tools</li>
<li>Worm modules propagate the malware: a WhatsApp bot and an Outlook email bot</li>
<li>All C2 and distribution infrastructure is hosted on Cloudflare Workers under a single account, with developer artifacts (debug logging paths, test process names) and an incomplete phishing page, suggesting the campaign was identified in an early operational stage</li>
</ul>
<h2 class="font-bold text-2xl md:text-4xl relative"><span id="delivery" class="absolute -top-32"></span>Delivery</h2>
<p>TCLBANKER is a Brazilian banking trojan that contains a dynamic infection chain with a heavy anti-analysis loading component that can deploy two embedded payloads (worm, banker). The observed infection chain bundles a malicious MSI installer inside a ZIP file. These MSI installer packages are abusing a signed Logitech program called <a href="https://www.logitech.com/en-us/software/logi-ai-prompt-builder">Logi AI Prompt Builder</a>.</p>
<p></p>
<p>TCLBANKER abuses DLL sideloading against <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">LogiAiPromptBuilder.exe</code>, a legitimate Logitech application built on the <a href="https://flutter.dev/">Flutter</a> framework. The malicious DLL <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">screen_retriever_plugin.dll</code> masquerades as a legitimate Flutter plugin of the same name and is loaded automatically when the host application starts.</p>
<p></p>
<p>After the MSI installation, the malicious DLL is immediately loaded and starts at the DllMain entry point.</p>
<h2 class="font-bold text-2xl md:text-4xl relative"><span id="loader" class="absolute -top-32"></span>Loader</h2>
<p>The loader component for TCLBANKER is packed with features, including anti-debugging features, anti-analysis checks, string encryption, system language checks, ETW patching, and a watchdog capability. While it has many features, it lacks depth and has references to older malware analysis tooling. It’s not entirely clear whether the developer used LLM-assisted workflows, but our team wouldn’t be surprised if that were the case.</p>
<p>At the beginning of the execution, TCLBANKER aligns the corresponding .NET assembly payloads based on whether the string (<code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">--renderer=sw</code>) is used in the command-line. Within its main loader function, it first performs allow-list/blocklist operations based on how the DLL was loaded. The malicious DLL will only execute if the host process comes from the following two processes:</p>
<ul>
<li><code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">logiaipromptbuilder.exe</code></li>
<li><code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">tclloader.exe</code> (Possible reference to developer string during testing)</li>
</ul>
<p>If the DLL was loaded by the following processes, it will refuse to run. These processes are traditionally used by analysts to load and debug DLLs.</p>
<ul>
<li><code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">rundll32.exe</code></li>
<li><code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">regsvr32.exe</code></li>
<li><code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">dllhost.exe</code></li>
<li><code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">svchost.exe</code></li>
</ul>
<p>Next, TCLBBANKER removes any user-mode hooking by replacing <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">ntdll.dll</code> from disk. For more evasion, the malware generates the following syscall trampolines used later:</p>
<ul>
<li><code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">NtQueryInformationProcess</code></li>
<li><code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">NtSetInformationThread</code></li>
<li><code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">NtSetInformationProcess</code></li>
<li><code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">NtTerminateProcess</code></li>
<li><code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">NtAllocateVirtualMemory</code></li>
<li><code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">NtProtectVirtualMemory</code></li>
</ul>
<p>After installing syscall stubs, the malware patches <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">EtwEventWrite</code> in <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">ntdll.dll</code> with the classic <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">xor eax, eax; ret</code> to disable user-mode ETW telemetry.</p>
<p></p>
<p>TCLBANKER performs an initial sandbox check by capturing a start tick using <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">GetTickCount64()</code>, sleeping for 500 ms, and measuring the elapsed time. If fewer than 450 ms have actually passed, the malware bails — this detects sandboxes or emulation frameworks that hook Sleep to return immediately..</p>
<p></p>
<p>One of the more interesting features of TCLBANKER is an enumeration function that generates three  fingerprints based on the following criteria:</p>
<ul>
<li>Anti-debugging checks</li>
<li>System disk information and memory checks</li>
<li>Language checks</li>
</ul>
<p>The developer uses magic constants assigned to “clean” paths for each category, then performs an XOR against each one to generate the environment hash. This environment hash value is significant because it affects downstream decryption of the embedded payload.</p>
<p></p>
<p>For example, if a debugger is present, it will produce an incorrect hash, so when the malware attempts to derive the decryption keys from the hash, the payload will not decrypt correctly, and TCLBANKER will stop executing.</p>
<p></p>
<h2 class="font-bold text-2xl md:text-4xl relative"><span id="anti-debugging-checks" class="absolute -top-32"></span>Anti-debugging checks</h2>
<p>TCLBANKER implements six different anti-debugging checks:</p>
<ul>
<li>Identify the debugger through the <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">Peb-&gt;BeingDebugged</code> flag</li>
<li>Checks heap-tail/heap-free/check-heap flags set when a process is launched under a debugger</li>
<li>Leverages <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">NtQueryInformationProcess()</code> using <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">ProcessDebugPort</code></li>
<li>Uses <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">NtQueryInformationProcess()</code> using <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">ProcessDebugObjectHandle</code></li>
<li>Hardware breakpoint detection via the debug registers (<code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">DR0-DR3</code>)</li>
<li>Measures the elapsed time using <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">QueryPerformanceCounter()</code> deltas and <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">RDTSC</code> cycle counts</li>
</ul>
<p></p>
<h2 class="font-bold text-2xl md:text-4xl relative"><span id="system-information-checks" class="absolute -top-32"></span>System information checks</h2>
<p>TCLBANKER has the following five different checks based on virtualization, system, and user information:</p>
<ul>
<li>Checks for virtualization software using vendor signature</li>
</ul>
<div class="table-container"><table style="width:100%;table-layout:fixed;word-wrap:break-word"><thead><tr><th style="text-align:center">Hypervisor</th><th style="text-align:center">Vendor signature</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td style="text-align:center">VMware</td><td style="text-align:center">VMwareVMware</td></tr><tr><td style="text-align:center">VirtualBox</td><td style="text-align:center">VBoxVBoxVBox</td></tr><tr><td style="text-align:center">KVM</td><td style="text-align:center">KVMKVMKVM</td></tr><tr><td style="text-align:center">Xen</td><td style="text-align:center">XenVMMXenVMM</td></tr><tr><td style="text-align:center">Parallels</td><td style="text-align:center">prl hyperv</td></tr><tr><td style="text-align:center">QEMU/TCG</td><td style="text-align:center">TCGTCGTCGTCG</td></tr></tbody></table></div>
<ul>
<li>Verify the root system drive (<code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">C:\\</code>) via <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">GetDiskFreeSpaceExW()</code> has at least 64 GB</li>
<li>Calls <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">GlobalMemoryStatusEx()</code> to verify the system has more than 2 GB of RAM</li>
<li>Checks for 2 or CPU processors via <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">GetSystemInfo()</code></li>
<li>Checks for generic sandbox/malware usernames<!-- -->
<ul>
<li><code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">sandbox</code>, <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">malware</code>, <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">virus</code>, <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">sample</code>, <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">john doe</code>, <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">currentuser</code></li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<p></p>
<h2 class="font-bold text-2xl md:text-4xl relative"><span id="language-checks" class="absolute -top-32"></span>Language checks</h2>
<p>For the last environment fingerprint check, TCLBANKER retrieves geographical information of the infected machine using <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">GetUserGeoID()</code>, targeting Brazilian users based on the geographical ID (<code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">0x20</code>). A second locale check via <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">GetUserDefaultLCID()</code> also ensures the user&#x27;s default language is Brazilian Portuguese (pt-BR, LANGID 0x0416).</p>
<p></p>
<p>After these sets of checks, TCLBANKER will either bail out of execution if anything is detected or, if not, produce another anti-debugging check by patching <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">DbgUiRemoteBreakin()</code>. The malware patches its first byte to <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">a ret</code> instruction so that any attempt to remotely break into the process does nothing — the injected thread immediately returns, and the target keeps running, unsuspended.</p>
<p></p>
<p>After this, the malware derives an AES-256 CBC key and IV by using hard-coded constants from the <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">.rdata</code> section along with the environmental hash calculated earlier. TCLBanker uses <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">BCryptDecrypt()</code> to decrypt the embedded payload, then decompresses via <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">RtlDecompressBuffer</code> using the LZNT1 compression algorithm.</p>
<p>Once the respective payload is decrypted, TCLBANKER initializes COM via <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">CoInitializeEx()</code> and uses the CLR hosting APIs to load the .NET runtime in-process. Before launching the payload entry point, TCLBanker creates two new threads: one serves as the watchdog, and the other monitors the watchdog thread as a heartbeat check.</p>
<h2 class="font-bold text-2xl md:text-4xl relative"><span id="watchdog" class="absolute -top-32"></span>Watchdog</h2>
<p>TCLBANKER has a comprehensive watchdog feature that targets various analysis tools, including disassemblers, debuggers, instrumentation products, anti-virus products, and sandbox products. This section will outline the various techniques used by this feature:</p>
<ul>
<li>Debugger check via <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">PEB→BeingDebugged</code></li>
<li>Watches for hardware breakpoints <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">DR0</code>/<code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">DR1</code>/<code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">DR2</code>/<code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">DR3</code></li>
<li>Checks Windows functions (<code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">BCryptDecrypt()</code>, <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">BCryptOpenAlgorithmProvider()</code>) for in-line hooks by scanning the first 12 bytes of each function</li>
<li>Monitors for instrumentation tools and related strings (<code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">frida</code>, <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">cydia</code>, <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">user-path injection</code>, <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">hook framework</code>)</li>
<li>Reviews all kernel named pipes searching for <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">frida</code> or <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">linjector</code></li>
<li>Performs process enumeration via <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">CreateToolhelp32Snapshot()</code> targeting the following process names:<!-- -->
<ul>
<li><code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">frida</code>, <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose <li>Checks for the following loaded modules<!-- -->

<li>Targets the following mutexes and events:<!-- -->
<ul>
<li><code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">Ida_trusted_idbs</code>, <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">IDA_COMM_PIPE_</code>, <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">Local\\x64dbg</code>, <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">Local\\x32dbg</code>, <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">Frida</code>, <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">YOURAPPNAMEHERE</code></li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Performs <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">CRC32</code> integrity check on the <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">.text</code> section to prevent any tampering</li>
</ul>
<h1 class="font-bold leading-tighter text-3xl md:text-5xl relative"><span id="banking-trojan-module" class="absolute -top-32"></span>Banking Trojan Module</h1>
<p><code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">Tcl.Agent</code> is a banking trojan, the main component of the chain. It is .NET Reactor-protected, and although we failed to deobfuscate it using available open-source tooling such as de4dot and NETReactorSlayer, we managed to statically deobfuscate this stage up to a satisfiable state using a custom deobfuscation pipeline to tackle .NET Reactor’s string encryption, control flow flattening, IL mutation, delegate proxies, and encrypted method bodies (Necrobit). Although it is a new malware, much of the code structure still follows ESET’s LATAM banking trojan <a href="https://web-assets.esetstatic.com/wls/2020/09/ESET_LATAM_financial_cybercrime.pdf">implementation blueprint</a>, published in 2020.</p>
<p>At start, the malware performs geofencing, requiring &gt;= 2 of the following indicators to match Brazil; otherwise, it exits immediately if not on a Brazilian machine:</p>
<div class="table-container"><table style="width:100%;table-layout:fixed;word-wrap:break-word"><thead><tr><th style="text-align:left">Check</th><th style="text-align:left">Implementation</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td style="text-align:left">Region Code</td><td style="text-align:left">new RegionInfo(CultureInfo.CurrentCulture.LCID).TwoLetterISORegionName == &quot;BR&quot;</td></tr><tr><td style="text-align:left">Timezone</td><td style="text-align:left">TimeZoneInfo.Local.BaseUtcOffset.TotalHours: if &gt;= -5.0, check if == -2.0</td></tr><tr><td style="text-align:left">LCID</td><td style="text-align:left">CultureInfo.CurrentCulture.LCID == 1046 (Portuguese-Brazil)</td></tr><tr><td style="text-align:left">Keyboard</td><td style="text-align:left">GetKeyboardLayoutList() - check each layout: (ToInt32() &amp; 0xFFFF) == 1046</td></tr></tbody></table></div>
<h2 class="font-bold text-2xl md:text-4xl relative"><span id="installation-and-persistence" class="absolute -top-32"></span>Installation and Persistence</h2>
<p>On the first run, the malware copies the entire application directory into <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">%LocalAppData%\LogiAI</code>. It computes a SHA-256 hash over all <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">.dll</code> and <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">.exe</code> files in the source directory and writes it to a <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">.version</code> marker file. On subsequent runs, it compares hashes to skip redundant copies. After copying, it launches the new instance from the install path and exits.</p>
<p>It creates a scheduled task named <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">RuntimeOptimizeService</code> using COM interop with the Task Scheduler (<code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">CLSID 0F87369F-A4E5-4CFC-BD3E-73E6154572DD</code>). The task is configured as hidden, enabled, with no execution time limit, allowed on battery, start-when-available, and fires on a logon trigger (<code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">type 9</code>) scoped to the current user. It registers with <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">TASK_CREATE_OR_UPDATE</code> and <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">TASK_LOGON_SERVICE_ACCOUNT</code>.</p>
<p></p>
<p>After persistence is established, the agent sends a first-run POST beacon to <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">https://campanha1-api.ef971a42.workers[.]dev/api/installs</code> with the agentId (<code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">MachineName-UserName</code>), MachineName, UserName (redundant), and the OS version. The request is authenticated with a hardcoded campaign authentication token <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">0d21613a-2609-45fc-83ff-d0feaa0c891f</code>. The newer variant adds debug logging around this call (<code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">C:\temp\tcl-debug.txt</code>), a developer artifact that inadvertently exposes agent presence on disk.</p>
<p></p>
<h2 class="font-bold text-2xl md:text-4xl relative"><span id="self-update" class="absolute -top-32"></span>Self-Update</h2>
<p>The agent implements a hash-based self-update gate that runs early in the startup pipeline. It reads a local version hash from <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">flutter_engine.cfg</code> in its install directory (migrating from a legacy <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">version.hash</code> filename if present), then fetches the current hash from the file server endpoint <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">documents.ef971a42.workers[.]dev/api/version</code> using a truncated User-Agent string <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">(Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36</code>.</p>
<p>The response is parsed for the &quot;hash&quot; key. If the remote hash matches the local hash, execution continues normally. On first install, the remote hash is written to disk, and execution proceeds without updating.</p>
<p></p>
<p>When a hash mismatch is detected, the agent downloads the update payload from <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">documents.ef971a42.workers[.]dev/api/update</code> as an MSI to <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">%TEMP%\update_{8hexchars}.msi</code>, authenticated with Bearer token <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">b7ba9e80-0d04-4d9e-b217-c8b3cce335a2</code>.</p>
<p></p>
<p>The download is validated against a 100KB minimum size as a sanity check. The agent then writes a self-deleting batch script to <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">%TEMP%</code> that polls the tasklist until the current process exits, executes <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">msiexec /i /qn REINSTALLMODE=amus</code> for silent installation, and deletes itself. The batch file is launched via a hidden <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">cmd.exe</code> process before the agent terminates, handing off execution to the updated payload.</p>
<h2 class="font-bold text-2xl md:text-4xl relative"><span id="browser-url-monitor-and-c2-session-initialization" class="absolute -top-32"></span>Browser URL Monitor and C2 Session Initialization</h2>
<p>Every second, the malware agent calls a browser URL monitor function that reads the foreground browser&#x27;s address bar via <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/framework/ui-automation/ui-automation-overview">UI Automation</a>. It calls <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">GetForegroundWindow</code>, resolves the owning process, checks the process name against Chrome, Firefox, Microsoft Edge, Brave, Opera, and Vivaldi, then uses <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">AutomationElement.FromHandle -&gt; FindFirst(Descendants, ControlType.Edit) -&gt; ValuePattern.Current.Value</code> to extract the URL, similar to this Stack Overflow <a href="https://stackoverflow.com/questions/5317642/retrieve-current-url-from-c-sharp-windows-forms-application/5318791#5318791">implementation</a>.</p>
<p></p>
<p>The extracted URL is matched against a fixed list of targeted banks embedded in the binary, encoded via XOR with a 16-byte key and base64 encoding.</p>
<p></p>
<p>This <a href="https://gist.github.com/jiayuchann/e298effb68bd472c9e577a630d0ceb20">GitHub Gist</a> contains a list of 59 targeted domains, including Brazilian banking, fintech platforms, and cryptocurrency exchanges, grouped by the target IDs appended to each decrypted domain.</p>
<p>When a match hits, the domain target ID is passed to the next state, which initializes the official C2 communication by establishing a WebSocket connection to <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">wss://mxtestacionamentos[.]com/ws</code>. The <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">OnConnect</code> handler fires, sending a registration packet containing the agent ID (a random GUID at runtime), MachineName, UserName, machine info, timestamp, domain target ID (so the C2 knows which website the victim opened), and a signature.</p>
<p>To produce a handshake signature, HMAC-SHA256 is used to sign the victim identifier (agent ID, MachineName, UserName, OSVersion, timestamp) using the campaign GUID <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">70e4f943-e323-4484-97d7-35401bf6812c</code> as the key.</p>
<p></p>
<p>The server then responds with a registration acknowledgment, officially starting the session, and enters the command dispatch loop. At session start, a Task Manager killer is fired every 500ms to prevent the victim from inspecting or terminating the agent&#x27;s process.</p>
<p></p>

<h2 class="font-bold text-2xl md:text-4xl relative"><span id="social-engineering-ui-framework" class="absolute -top-32"></span>Social Engineering UI Framework</h2>
<p>A more interesting capability of the banking trojan is a <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/overview/">WPF-based</a> full-screen overlay subsystem that orchestrates bank-themed fraud flows during active C2 sessions.</p>
<h3 class="font-bold leading-tight text-xl md:text-3xl relative"><span id="overlay-lifecycle" class="absolute -top-32"></span>Overlay Lifecycle</h3>
<p>The overlay manager spawns one full-screen WPF window per monitor. Windows are configured as borderless, topmost, and hidden from the taskbar (<code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">WindowStyle.None</code>, <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">Topmost = true</code>, <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">ShowInTaskbar = false</code>), with a custom <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">Closing</code> handle that refuses dismissal until an internal flag is flipped by the operator through the overlay teardown command, preventing the windows from being closed.</p>
<p></p>
<p></p>
<p>At startup, the manager captures a PNG screenshot of every display via <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">CopyFromScreen</code> as the overlay backdrop, creating a “frozen desktop” look. Depending on the currently active overlay, the victim perceives their real desktop environment behind it.</p>
<p>A <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">500ms</code> timer continuously <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">HWND_TOPMOST</code> via <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">SetWindowPos</code> to defeat any window attempting to surface above the overlay.</p>
<p></p>
<p>In addition, an anti-capture feature calls <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">SetWindowDisplayAffinity</code> with <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">WDA_EXCLUDEFROMCAPTURE</code>, rendering the overlay invisible to any screen-capturing tools, allowing the operator to see through their own overlay through the screenshot and screenstreaming commands.</p>
<p></p>
<h3 class="font-bold leading-tight text-xl md:text-3xl relative"><span id="input-blocker" class="absolute -top-32"></span>Input Blocker</h3>
<p>On the primary monitor, two hooks are installed: <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">WH_KEYBOARD_LL</code> and <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">WH_MOUSE_LL</code>. Both hooks check their respective injected flags (<code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">LLKHF_INJECTED</code> for keyboard, <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">LLMHF_INJECTED</code> for mouse), allowing input injected via <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">SendInput</code> by the operator’s remote commands to pass through untouched. The keyboard hook swallows Tab, Escape, Alt+F4, Win keys, PrintScreen, Ctrl, Alt, and all navigation keys; the mouse hook blocks right-click, middle-click, and scroll, but allows left-click and movement, so the victim can still interact with the overlay prompts.</p>
<p></p>
<h3 class="font-bold leading-tight text-xl md:text-3xl relative"><span id="social-engineering-ui-builders" class="absolute -top-32"></span>Social Engineering UI Builders</h3>
<p>Five interchangeable content renderers plug into the overlay framework:</p>
<p>Credential Prompt: Supports three input modes, selected based on the operator&#x27;s request parameters.</p>
<ul>
<li>Phone mode applies real-time Brazilian format masking ((##) ####-#### for 10-digit landlines, (##) #####-#### for 11-digit mobiles) with max 11 digits.</li>
<li>Virtual keypad mode renders an on-screen numeric keypad (buttons 0–9 plus &quot;limpar&quot;/clear), displaying input as bullet characters to mimic PIN entry.</li>
<li>Default mode accepts plain text with a configurable max length.</li>
</ul>
<p>All modes run input through a quality validator that algorithmically rejects same-digit sequences (<code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">000000</code>) and ascending/descending runs (<code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">123456</code>, <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">654321</code>) to prevent victims from entering throwaway values.</p>
<p>The submit action fires the captured values to the C2.</p>
<p></p>
<p>Vishing Wait Screen: Triggers after the victim submits their phone number in the credential prompt. Displays &quot;Estamos entrando em contato&quot; (&quot;We are getting in touch&quot;) with a central image “breathing” animation and three dots with staggered opacity animations (<code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">300ms</code> offset per dot) producing a &quot;connecting&quot; visual. The operator or an accomplice can then call the victim&#x27;s real phone, impersonating bank security staff.</p>
<p></p>
<p>Progress Steps: A fully operator-templated stall screen displaying a list of fake processing steps with a randomized animation. Step durations are randomized to total approximately 15 minutes. A timer advances through each step sequentially, visually marking completed steps, highlighting the current one, and dimming the remaining ones. When all steps are complete, the sequence resets to an earlier position with new randomized timings and continues.</p>
<p>Fake Windows Update: An alternative stall screen mimicking the Windows 10/11 update-restart screen. Renders a solid <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">#0078D7</code> (Windows accent blue) background with a five-ellipse spinning indicator arranged in a circle. A percentage readout jumps by a random 25–35% at randomly selected 50–81-second intervals to mimic the irregular progress behavior of real Windows Updates. Default subtitle: &quot;Trabalhando em atualizacoes&quot; (&quot;Working on updates&quot;).</p>
<p></p>
<p>Cutout Overlay: Cuts a rectangular hole in the full-screen overlay, exposing the underlying application window. The operator specifies hole dimensions via opcode 87, in which the overlay manager builds a themed card with a transparent-border placeholder, computes its screen coordinates post-layout, and cuts a matching region hole using <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">CreateRectRgn + CombineRgn(RGN_DIFF) + SetWindowRgn</code>. The target window is repositioned underneath the hole. The result is a real application window framed within the overlay, and the victim interacts with the actual application while the surrounding overlay provides deceptive context.</p>
<p></p>
<h1 class="font-bold leading-tighter text-3xl md:text-5xl relative"><span id="worm-module" class="absolute -top-32"></span>Worm module</h1>
<p>The second module invoked by the loader is <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">Tcl.WppBot</code>, is designed to propagate spam and phishing messages at scale, to distribute TCLBANKER. Two distinct agent types were recovered from two different loaders and analyzed:</p>
<ul>
<li>A WhatsApp worm that hijacks browser sessions</li>
<li>An Outlook email bot that abuses Microsoft Outlook through COM interop</li>
</ul>
<p><code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">Tcl.WppBot</code> is also .NET Reactor-protected with the same version used to protect <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">Tcl.Agent</code>, and so we also managed to statically deobfuscate payloads in this stage.</p>
<p>Both agents share the same C2 backend, authentication credentials, and operational infrastructure. The C2 URL and API key are decrypted at startup using XOR decryption with a hardcoded key.</p>
<ul>
<li>C2 URL: <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">campanha1-api.ef971a42.workers[.]dev</code> (Cloudflare Workers app)</li>
<li>API key / Bearer token: <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">0d21613a-2609-45fc-83ff-d0feaa0c891f</code></li>
</ul>
<p></p>
<p>The C2 serves a single superset campaign configuration object via the <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">https://campanha1-api.ef971a42.workers[.]dev/api/campaign</code> endpoint. Each agent variant deserializes the full object but only reads the fields relevant to its channel.</p>
<p>Captured configuration:</p>

<p>The same Cloudflare account <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">ef971a42</code> also hosts the payload delivery CDN (domain for <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">fileUrl</code> in the configuration object) at <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">documents.ef971a42.workers[.]dev</code>. Accessible through the <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">/file</code> endpoint, it currently serves a zip file containing the TCLBANKER-trojanized LogiAI Prompt Builder MSI. This infrastructure decision allows the operator to rapidly redeploy infrastructure without maintaining dedicated servers.</p>
<p></p>
<p>As of the time of writing, the phishing domain <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">arquivos-omie[.]com</code> identified in the configuration above, created on 2026-04-15, is not at an operable state (Welcome! This portal is currently undergoing scheduled maintenance. Please try again later.) The campaign could be in its early operational stages or staged for tasking. This domain is also named to impersonate a popular Brazilian Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) suite.</p>
<p></p>
<h2 class="font-bold text-2xl md:text-4xl relative"><span id="agent-1-whatsapp-bot" class="absolute -top-32"></span>Agent 1: WhatsApp Bot</h2>
<p>The WhatsApp agent silently takes over the victim’s authenticated WhatsApp Web session to send spam messages and distribute TCLBANKER to Brazilian contacts.</p>
<h3 class="font-bold leading-tight text-xl md:text-3xl relative"><span id="session-hijacking" class="absolute -top-32"></span>Session Hijacking</h3>
<p>The malware starts by discovering Chromium-based browsers on the target system, then scanning both the <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">App Paths</code> registry entries and common installation directories for Chrome, Edge, Brave, Opera, and Vivaldi. It then walks each browser&#x27;s user profiles (e.g., &quot;Default,&quot; &quot;Profile 1,&quot; etc.), looking for evidence of an active WhatsApp Web session. A profile is flagged as having an authenticated session if its IndexedDB storage contains the WhatsApp Web LevelDB directory at <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">&lt;profile_dir&gt;/IndexedDB/https_web.whatsapp[.]com_0.indexeddb.leveldb/</code>.</p>
<p>Then each profile is sent to the profile-cloning and session-hijacking function.</p>
<p></p>
<p>For each qualifying profile, the malware clones it to a temporary directory at <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">%TEMP%\&lt;GUID&gt;\</code>, copying only the files needed to resume the WhatsApp Web session: <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">IndexedDB</code>, <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">Local Storage</code>, <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">Session Storage</code>, <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">databases</code>, <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">Web Data</code>, <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">Login Data</code>, and <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">Cookies</code>. It then launches a headless Chromium instance via Selenium WebDriver, with <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">--user-data-dir</code> pointing at the cloned profile.</p>
<p>The matching <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">chromedriver.exe</code> is resolved at runtime by a disguised Selenium Manager binary dropped at <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">%TEMP%\msvc-rt14\bin\hostfxr.exe</code>, which is invoked with <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">--browser chrome --output json</code> and returns the path of a chromedriver compatible with the victim&#x27;s installed Chrome version.</p>
<p></p>
<p>Immediately after launch, the malware injects JavaScript to bypass bot-detection frameworks by hiding <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">navigator.webdriver</code>, populates <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">chrome.runtime</code>, reconciles the <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">Notification.permission</code> / <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">permissions.query</code> state mismatch, fakes a non-empty <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">navigator.plugins</code> array, and sets <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">navigator.languages</code> to <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">[&#x27;pt-BR&#x27;, &#x27;pt&#x27;, &#x27;en-US&#x27;, &#x27;en&#x27;]</code> to match the target demographic.</p>
<pre><code>Object.defineProperty(navigator, &#x27;webdriver&#x27;, {
    get: () = &gt; undefined 
}

);

if (window.chrome)  {

    runtime: {}

};</code></pre>
<p>With the cloned profile loaded, the browser navigates to <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">web.whatsapp[.]com</code>, and the malware waits up to 45 seconds to observe the resulting page state. If the chat interface appears (the cloned IndexedDB was valid and the session resumed without a QR scan), it injects an embedded WA-JS (<a href="https://github.com/wppconnect-team/wppconnect">WPPConnect</a>) library and waits for <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">WPP.contact.list</code> and <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">WPP.chat.sendTextMessage</code> to become callable before starting the campaign dispatch loop. If the QR code prompt is shown instead, the engine returns <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">&quot;qr_code&quot;</code> without attempting injection, then tries the next candidate profile.</p>
<p></p>
<h3 class="font-bold leading-tight text-xl md:text-3xl relative"><span id="spam-functionality" class="absolute -top-32"></span>Spam Functionality</h3>
<p>Once the injection succeeds, the malware retrieves the active campaign from the C2 endpoint <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">https://campanha1-api.ef971a42.workers[.]dev/api/campaign</code>, which supplies the message body, optional attachment URL, caption, and timing parameters. TCLBANKER is then downloaded from the file server at <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">https://documents.ef971a42.workers[.]dev/file</code> and reconstructed in the browser context as a <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/File/File">File object</a>, without being dropped to disk.</p>
<p>The malware then calls <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">WPP.contact.list</code> to harvest the victim&#x27;s address book, filters out groups, broadcasts, and non-Brazilian numbers, and begins dispatching messages through <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">WPP.chat.sendTextMessage</code> and <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">sendFileMessage</code>. The malware reports progress to the C2 endpoint <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">/api/progress</code> after each batch, and polls <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">/api/control</code> for remote pause or resend commands from the operator.</p>
<h2 class="font-bold text-2xl md:text-4xl relative"><span id="agent-2-outlook-email-bot" class="absolute -top-32"></span>Agent 2: Outlook Email Bot</h2>
<p>The Outlook agent is an email spambot that abuses the victim’s installed Microsoft Outlook application to send phishing emails from the victim’s email address, making them harder to detect as spam than emails sent from attacker-controlled infrastructure.</p>
<h3 class="font-bold leading-tight text-xl md:text-3xl relative"><span id="outlook-discovery--com-attachment" class="absolute -top-32"></span>Outlook Discovery &amp; COM Attachment</h3>
<p>If <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">OUTLOOK.EXE</code> is not already running, it attempts to locate the installation in <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">App Paths</code> registry entries and known installation directories and launches it in a new process. The malware then attaches to the process via COM interop: <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/office/vba/outlook/how-to/security/obtain-and-log-on-to-an-instance-of-outlook"><code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">Marshal.GetActiveObject(&quot;Outlook.Application&quot;)</code></a>, and validates that it has at least one email account configured.</p>
<h3 class="font-bold leading-tight text-xl md:text-3xl relative"><span id="contact-harvesting" class="absolute -top-32"></span>Contact Harvesting</h3>
<p>The malware then drops a PowerShell script, <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">%TEMP%\oc&lt;guid&gt;.ps1,</code> that harvests contacts via Outlook COM from a separate process. It harvests contacts from two sources: first, it reads the default Contacts folder for all contact entries, extracting email addresses and full names from each contact item. Second, it iterates every store’s root folders to find inbox-like folders, sorts inbox messages by latest, and extracts sender email addresses and names before writing them to a <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">.txt</code> file in <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">email|name</code> format.</p>
<p></p>
<p>For each candidate email, additional filtering is done to maximize deliverability.</p>
<p></p>
<h3 class="font-bold leading-tight text-xl md:text-3xl relative"><span id="spam-functionality-1" class="absolute -top-32"></span>Spam Functionality</h3>
<p>Similar to the WhatsApp bot, the malware retrieves the active campaign from <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">https://campanha1-api.ef971a42.workers[.]dev/api/campaign</code>, then sends emails through the victim&#x27;s own Outlook accounts via COM automation. Each email is constructed via <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">outlookApp.CreateItem(0)</code> (<code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">MailItem</code>) with the recipient in <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">To</code>, the campaign subject line, and the campaign content <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">emailMessage</code>, sent using the victim&#x27;s actual account via <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">SendUsingAccount</code>.</p>
<p>Between sends, the agent applies a randomized delay and periodically checks the C2 control endpoint <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">/api/control</code> for pause or resend commands, and reports progress to <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">/api/progress</code>.</p>
<h1 class="font-bold leading-tighter text-3xl md:text-5xl relative"><span id="infrastructure" class="absolute -top-32"></span>Infrastructure</h1>
<p>The REF3076 actors have leveraged the <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">worker[.]dev</code> Cloudflare Serverless infrastructure for C2 and file hosting. This decision allows them to inherit any trust victims might already have in Cloudflare and to rotate infrastructure quickly as needed.</p>
<p>Pivoting on the body-hash (<code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">91fafaa1240676afe5c55d931261e3798797c408</code>) of the phishing site above (<code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">arquivos-omie[.]com</code>), we were able to identify additional domains that are likely being prepared for weaponization:</p>
<div class="table-container"><table style="width:100%;table-layout:fixed;word-wrap:break-word"><thead><tr><th style="text-align:left">Domain</th><th style="text-align:left">First Seen</th><th style="text-align:left">Info</th><th style="text-align:left">ASN (Providor)</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td style="text-align:left">arquivos-omie[.]com</td><td style="text-align:left">2026-04-17</td><td style="text-align:left">Squatting - Brazilian SaaS for SMBs</td><td style="text-align:left">AS 13335 (Cloudflare)</td></tr><tr><td style="text-align:left">documentos-online[.]com</td><td style="text-align:left">2026-04-11</td><td style="text-align:left">Generic</td><td style="text-align:left">AS 13335 (Cloudflare)</td></tr><tr><td style="text-align:left">afonsoferragista[.]com</td><td style="text-align:left">2026-04-22</td><td style="text-align:left">Hardware store - Likely used in a B2B lure</td><td style="text-align:left">AS 13335 (Cloudflare)</td></tr><tr><td style="text-align:left">doccompartilhe[.]com</td><td style="text-align:left">2026-04-15</td><td style="text-align:left">Generic - “Shared a document”</td><td style="text-align:left">AS 13335 (Cloudflare)</td></tr><tr><td style="text-align:left">recebamais[.]com</td><td style="text-align:left">2026-04-20</td><td style="text-align:left">Squatting - Brazilian credit/loan brokerage</td><td style="text-align:left">AS 13335 (Cloudflare)</td></tr></tbody></table></div>
<p>More Brazilian phishing infrastructure was discovered after a broader pivot in the banner title (<code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">Portal</code> <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">Corporativo</code>), but it’s unclear whether it was directly related to REF3076 or to other actors in the Latin American banking trojan ecosystem. Notably, one cluster leveraged the Cloudflare <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">pages[.]dev</code> free static-site hosting product.</p>
<p>The C2 domain <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">mxtestacionamentos[.]com</code> previously pointed to a Brazilian-hosted IP <code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">191.96.224[.]96</code>.</p>
<p></p>
<p>Last year, this IP concurrently hosted a REF3076 C2 domain, a REF3076 phishing domain, and a domain previously <a href="https://www.trendmicro.com/en_gb/research/25/j/self-propagating-malware-spreads-via-whatsapp.html">associated with the Water Saci campaign</a> and SORVEPOTEL/MAVERICK malware by TrendMicro (<code class="px-1.5 py-1 rounded not-prose bg-[var(--tw-prose-invert-pre-bg)] whitespace-break-spaces text-[85%] text-emerald-600">saogeraldoshiping[.]com</code>).</p>
<p></p>
<h1 class="font-bold leading-tighter text-3xl md:text-5xl relative"><span id="conclusion" class="absolute -top-32"></span>Conclusion</h1>
<p>TCLBANKER reflects a broader maturation happening across the Brazilian banking trojan ecosystem. Techniques that were once the hallmark of more sophisticated threat actors: environment-gated payload decryption, direct syscall generation, real-time social engineering orchestration over WebSocket, are now being packaged into commodity crimeware. The barrier to entry continues to drop, especially when powerful LLMs are readily accessible for code generation.</p>
<p>The inclusion of self-propagating worm modules marks a notable shift in this space. The campaign inherits the trust and deliverability of legitimate communications by hijacking victims&#x27; WhatsApp sessions and Outlook accounts. This is a distribution model that traditional email gateways and reputation-based defenses are ill-equipped to catch. As Latin American banking trojans continue to adopt these self-spreading mechanisms, organizations should expect the volume and reach of these campaigns to scale accordingly.</p>
<p>Developer artifacts throughout the chain, including debug logging paths, test process names, and a phishing site still under construction, suggest REF3076 is in its early operational stages. This is a campaign still being built out, not wound down.</p>
